summary: Our project focuses on the Moon and Mars, aiming to provide an immersive and detailed exploration of the technological vehicles, equipment, and tools used bv NASA in the past and present, as well as those that have been forgotten or left behind.It allows you to examine and discover these technologies through detailed models, learn their complete stories from their initial design and construction to 3D their eventual abandonment on the desolate surfaces of these planets, and explore and understand every aspect of them down to the smallest detail
details:
Project: Abandoned But Not Forgotten – Moon & Mars Heritage Observatory

What is this project, in one sentence?

It is a website where anyone can explore, in 3D, the spacecraft that humanity sent to the Moon and Mars and then left there forever.

The problem we want to solve

Since 1959, people have sent many robots and spacecraft to the Moon and Mars. Some of them crashed on purpose. Some landed and worked for years. Some broke, lost power, or simply stopped talking to Earth. When a mission ends, the spacecraft does not disappear. It stays on the surface, exactly where it stopped. But its story slowly disappears from people’s memory. The information about these spacecraft exists, but it is spread across many technical archives that are hard for normal people to read. Most students today have never heard of Spirit, Surveyor 3 or Beagle 2. We think these machines are part of human history, like old ships or ancient monuments. They deserve to be remembered and protected.

Our solution

We built an interactive “observatory” that runs in any web browser. You do not need to install anything. You open the website and you see a realistic 3D Moon. With one click, you can switch to Mars. On each planet, small markers show where real spacecraft are lying today, placed at their real latitude and longitude. In total, the site has 13 objects on the Moon and 14 on Mars.

What happens when you open the website?

Cinematic opening: While the website loads, you watch a short animation of the real LCROSS mission. The percentage counter goes from 0 to 100, and the spacecraft flies closer to the Moon’s south pole at the same time. Real-looking numbers show altitude, speed and time to impact. At 100%, it hits the Cabeus crater. You see a flash of light, shockwaves and flying moon dust. LCROSS really did this in 2009 to search for water ice.

Clean main screen: The dust clears and the main observatory appears. You see only the planet and a big title, so nothing distracts you.

Scroll to learn: When you scroll down, the information comes section by section, like a documentary: an overview of the planet, the details of the selected spacecraft, its 3D model, a full catalogue with search and filters, a timeline from 1957 to 2026, and the sources. Small dots on the right side show which section you are in. You can click them to jump between sections.

What can you do with each spacecraft?

When you click a spacecraft, you see:

its launch date, arrival date and last signal date

why the mission ended and why it matters for science

a 3D model you can rotate and zoom

a landing animation based on how that mission really arrived: parachute, airbags, rocket engines, or a direct crash

For Apollo 11 and 17, Viking 1 and 2, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight, the Ingenuity helicopter (with spinning rotors) and Mars Global Surveyor, we use official NASA 3D models. For spacecraft with no official NASA model, such as Luna 2 or Lunokhod, we built our own detailed models.

Real NASA data

The Moon: covered with real NASA data from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), using the CGI Moon Kit: the LROC color map and the LOLA elevation map. Craters, dark “seas” and mountains are in their true places, and their shadows change with the light.

Mars: uses a NASA global color map. Valles Marineris, Olympus Mons and the polar ice caps are visible in their real positions.

Mission facts: dates and facts come from NASA archives such as NSSDCA and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal. Locations are checked with the USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature and orbital images from MRO HiRISE.

Why is it important?

NASA has published recommendations to protect historic sites like the Apollo landing areas, and the US “One Small Step” Act (2020) made them a requirement for NASA partners. More countries and companies are going to the Moon now, so these sites need protection. You cannot protect something people do not know about. Our website makes these places visible, emotional and easy to understand, especially for students.

Who is it for?

Students, teachers, space fans, and anyone curious. The site works in 6 languages: Turkish, English, Hindi, Spanish, French and Russian.

Technology (simple version)

The site is built with HTML, JavaScript and three.js (a 3D library for the browser). Heavy visual effects run on the graphics card. NASA models and big textures load in the background, so the site opens fast. If a computer is slow, the site automatically lowers the image quality to stay smooth.

Future plans

We want to add deep-space probes such as Voyager 1 and 2, Pioneer, Cassini and Rosetta, so the observatory covers the whole Solar System.

Transparency about AI

We used Anthropic’s Claude AI assistant to help with interface development, data collection, 3D model conversion and visualization. We checked all mission data against official NASA and USGS sources. All sources are listed on the website.
